title: Bible Languages: Biblical Hebrew, Koine Greek and Latin
subtitle: Alphabets, grammar, core vocabulary, everyday phrases and how to translate between the three, with flashcards and an interlinear reader
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A beginner-friendly course in the three languages of the Bible. Learn the Hebrew alphabet and vowels, the Greek alphabet and cases, and Latin nouns and verbs; build a core vocabulary of 45 words and 16 phrases side by side with memory hooks; read thirteen parallel passages with an interlinear reader; and practise translating between the languages with spaced-repetition flashcards and Python labs.

chapters.title: Three languages, one library

maps.title: The three languages

summary: The Bible was written mostly in Hebrew, with a little Aramaic, and the New Testament in Koine Greek. Early Greek and Latin translations, the Septuagint and the Vulgate, shaped the church for a thousand years and still hold many of its words.

The three languages work differently. Hebrew builds words from three-letter roots and reads right to left. Greek and Latin both use endings (cases) to show who does what to whom, so word order is flexible.
This course teaches the alphabets and sounds, the grammar, the core vocabulary side by side, common phrases, and how to translate between the three, with memory tools in every chapter.

glossary.def: The common Greek of the Mediterranean world, about 300 BC to 300 AD, the language of the New Testament.
The Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures, made in Alexandria from about 250 BC.
The Latin Bible translated mostly by Jerome around 400 AD.
A text with a word-by-word gloss written under each word of the original.
A word that shares an origin with a word in another language, like Latin pater (πατήρ) and English paternal.
In Hebrew, the usually three consonants that carry a word's core meaning.

keyPoints: Hebrew: right to left, consonants first, roots of three letters.
Greek: 24 letters, five cases, three genders, flexible word order.
Latin: no alphabet to learn, six cases, no articles, verb at the end.
A Greek or Latin ending tells you the job of the word; Hebrew uses small words and word order.
You learn fastest by short daily sessions, not long rare ones.
Link every new word to something you know: an English word, a picture or a story.

items: ELI5. The Bible comes in three languages, like a house with three doors. Hebrew is the old door, Greek the middle door and Latin the door to the west. You can go in through any one and find the same stories.

Imagine a library with three doors. Behind the first is Hebrew, the language of the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms. Behind the second is Koine Greek, the plain, widely spoken Greek in which the Gospels and letters were written.
Behind the third is Latin, the language of Rome and of the church in the West. Most of the Bible can be read in at least two of these, which is why learning them together pays off.

The Old Testament was written in Hebrew, with small parts in Aramaic. About 250 years before Christ, Jewish scholars in Alexandria translated it into Greek, the Septuagint. The New Testament was written in Greek, and the apostles often quote the Septuagint.
Around 400 AD Jerome translated the Bible into Latin, the Vulgate, working from the Hebrew and Greek. So the same verse often exists in all three, and we can lay them side by side.

The languages are built differently. Hebrew is a Semitic language, related to Arabic. It is written right to left, and a word grows from a root of usually three consonants. The root k-t-v means writing: katav (כָּתַב) is he wrote, ktav (כְּתָב) is a writing, sefer (סֵפֶר) is a book.

Greek and Latin are Indo-European, cousins of English. They show a word's job with an ending, called its case. In Latin, Deus creavit caelum and caelum creavit Deus both mean that God made heaven, because the endings say who is the subject.

How do you remember so many new words? Three tools run through the whole course. First, spaced repetition: review a word after one day, then two, then four, then eight. The flashcard labs use exactly this system, called Leitner boxes.

Second, hooks: tie each word to an English word, such as photo for the Greek phos, light, or pacify for the Latin pax, peace. Third, stories: a vivid little picture sticks far better than a bare list.

A word on pronunciation. Scholars read these languages in slightly different ways. This course uses a simple, widely used reading for each: standard modern Hebrew sounds, a school reading of Koine Greek, and the Latin of the Church, which is easy for English speakers.
Learn one way well, and the others follow quickly.

summary: Hebrew has 22 letters, all of them consonants, written and read from right to left. Five letters change shape at the end of a word. Letters double as numbers, so every word has a numeric value, called gematria.
A few letters sound alike (tet (ט) and tav (ת), kaf (כ) and qof (ק)). Learning each one with a picture-name and a sound makes them stick.
The labs match letters to sounds and compute gematria in Python.

glossary.def: The Hebrew alphabet, named for its first two letters, alef (א) and bet (ב).
A different shape for kaf (כ), mem (מ), nun (נ), pe (פ) and tsade (צ) at the end of a word.
The numeric value of a word, found by adding its letters' values.
A script that writes the consonants and leaves most vowels to the reader.
The six letters bet (ב), gimel (ג), dalet (ד), kaf (כ), pe (פ) and tav (ת), which can be hard or soft.

keyPoints: 22 letters, no capitals, read right to left.
Final forms: kaf ך, mem ם, nun ן, pe ף, tsade ץ.
Alef (א) and ayin (ע) are silent carriers of a vowel; chet (ח) is a rough h.
Vav ו and yod י can be vowel letters as well as consonants.
Values: alef (א) 1 to yod (י) 10, then 20, 30 ... 90, then 100 to 400 (qof (ק), resh (ר), shin (ש), tav (ת)).

items: ELI5. Hebrew letters are 22 little pictures, and you read them backwards from the right. Each letter is also a number, so every word hides a sum, like a secret code.

Open a Hebrew book at what an English reader calls the back. Hebrew starts at the right edge of the page and the line runs to the left. The alphabet has 22 letters, all consonants, and no capital letters.
The first four are alef (א), bet (ב), gimel (ג) and dalet (ד), which gave Greek its alpha, beta, gamma and delta, and gave us our A, B, C and D.

ט tet   t          | י yod  y/i     | כ kaf   k/kh| ל lamed l

items: Five letters have a second shape used only at the end of a word: kaf ך, mem ם, nun ן, pe ף and tsade ץ. The final forms reach below the line. This makes it easy to see where a word stops, since Hebrew has no space-saving capitals.
Some letters look alike, so learn them in pairs: bet ב has a rounded corner and kaf כ a round back; dalet ד and resh ר differ by a small corner; vav ו and zayin ז differ by a crown.

The letters bet (ב), gimel (ג), dalet (ד), kaf (כ), pe (פ) and tav (ת) can be hard or soft. Bet is b when it carries a dot called a dagesh and v without it. Kaf is k with a dagesh and kh without, and pe is p with a dagesh and f without.
The letter shin (ש) is sh with a dot on the right and s with a dot on the left, which is then called sin (שׂ).

Because Hebrew letters were also the numbers, every word has a value. Alef (א) is one, bet (ב) two, up to yod (י) ten, then tens up to tsade (צ) at ninety, then hundreds: qof (ק) one hundred, resh (ר) two hundred, shin (ש) three hundred, tav (ת) four hundred.
Shalom (שָׁלוֹם), shin lamed (ל) vav (ו) mem (מ).
Is 300 plus 30 plus 6 plus 40, which is 376. People have found hidden connections in such sums for centuries; here it is a fun way to drill the letters and the numbers.

Memory tip: say the letter names aloud in order, like a song, twice a day for a week. Then draw each letter once while saying its sound. The ancient letter pictures help too: alef (א) was an ox, bet (ב) a house, gimel (ג) a camel, dalet (ד) a door.

chapters.title: Hebrew: vowels and reading

maps.title: Reading Hebrew
links: Shva ◌ְ | is | A short e or silent

summary: Early Hebrew wrote only consonants. Later scribes added little dots and dashes, the niqqud (נִקּוּד), to show vowels. With them a beginner can read any word aloud.
There are five vowel sounds in several shapes, plus the half-vowel shva (◌ְ) and the dot called dagesh (◌ּ). Every syllable has exactly one vowel.
The labs match vowel signs to sounds and ask you to read real words.

glossary.def: The system of dots and dashes written with the consonants to mark vowels.
A sign that marks either a very short e or no vowel at all.
A dot inside a letter that makes it hard, or doubles it.
A beat of sound; in Hebrew each syllable has one vowel.
Letters like vav (ו) and yod (י) used to show vowels.

keyPoints: Vowel signs sit below, above or inside the consonant.
ַ patach (◌ַ) and ָ kamets (◌ָ) sound like ah; ֵ tsere (◌ֵ) and ֶ segol (◌ֶ) like eh.
ִ hiriq (◌ִ) is ee, ֹ holam (◌ֹ) is oh, ֻ kubbuts (◌ֻ) and וּ shureq (וּ) are oo.
ְ shva (◌ְ) at the start of a word is a quick e; between syllables it is silent.
Most words are stressed on the last syllable.

items: ELI5. Hebrew first wrote only the hard sounds, like a text message without vowels. Later people added dots and dashes so everybody could say the words the same way.

The earliest Hebrew texts have no vowel marks. Readers knew the words, so consonants were enough, as you can read 'Pls rd ths' in English. A few centuries after Christ, scribes called the Masoretes added a system of dots and dashes, the niqqud (נִקּוּד), to preserve the exact reading.
Printed Bibles and learner books still use it.

lesson.code:
ַ patach  ah  (בַּ ba)     ָ kamets ah  (בָּ ba)
ֵ tsere   ay  (בֵּ bay)    ֶ segol  eh  (בֶּ be)
ִ hiriq   ee  (בִּ bee)    ֹ holam  oh  (בֹּ bo)
ֻ kubbuts oo  (בֻּ boo)    וּ shureq oo (בוּ boo)
ְ shva    short e or silent

items: The sign sits under most letters, over a few, and inside the vav (ו). Say a consonant plus a vowel as one beat: bet (ב) plus kamets (◌ָ) is ba. Add the next letter, and you have a word: ba plus yod (י) plus tav (ת) gives bayit (בַּיִת), a house, from the vocabulary list.
Every syllable needs exactly one vowel sound, so count the vowels to count the beats.

The shva (◌ְ), two dots stacked under a letter, is the only sign that behaves in two ways. At the beginning of a word, or after a long vowel, it is a very short e as in the first syllable of the English word 'again'. After a short vowel it is silent and just closes the syllable. The dagesh (◌ּ).
A dot inside a letter, hardens the begadkefat letters and doubles other letters, as in the article ha plus a doubled letter.

Practice reading with words you already know. Shalom (שָׁלוֹם) is shin (ש) kamets (◌ָ), lamed (ל) holam (◌ֹ) vav (ו), mem (מ): sha-lom. Melekh (מֶלֶךְ), king, is mem segol (◌ֶ), lamed segol, final kaf (כ): me-lekh.

Elohim (אֱלֹהִים) has the alef (א) carrying a segol (the e), then a shva (◌ְ)-holam: e-lo-him. Say each aloud slowly three times, then at speed. Reading aloud is the best way to turn the signs into habit.

chapters.title: Hebrew grammar: nouns, articles and sentences

maps.title: Hebrew nouns
links: Verb to be | is left out | In the present

summary: Hebrew nouns are masculine or feminine and singular, plural or dual. The plural usually ends in -im for masculine and -ot for feminine, and pairs of things use the dual -ayim.

There is one article, ha- (הַ), meaning 'the'. There is no word for 'a'. The verb 'is' is usually left out: 'The man good' means 'the man is good'. Two nouns joined together, as in 'house of the king', form a construct chain.
Small words are attached to the front: ve- (וְ) and, be- (בְּ) in, le- (לְ) to or for, min (מִן) from. Pronouns can attach to the end: -i my, -kha your, -o his.

glossary.def: Whether a noun is masculine or feminine.
A special plural for natural pairs, ending in -ayim.
The word 'the'; in Hebrew the prefix ha- (הַ).
A noun linked to the noun that follows, meaning 'X of Y'.
A sentence with no verb, where 'is' is understood.
A short word, like be- (בְּ) or le- (לְ), written as part of the next word.

keyPoints: Masculine plural -im: melekh (מֶלֶךְ), melakhim (מְלָכִים) (kings).
Feminine often ends in -ah; plural -ot: torah (תּוֹרָה), torot (תּוֹרוֹת).
Dual -ayim: yad hand, yadayim (יָדַיִם) two hands; mayim (מַיִם), shamayim (שָׁמַיִם).
Definite: ha- (הַ) plus the noun, ha-melekh (הַמֶּלֶךְ) = the king. No word for 'a'.
Present 'is' is not written: ha-ish tov (הָאִישׁ טוֹב) means the man is good.
Construct: bet melekh (בֵּית מֶלֶךְ) = house of a king; devar adonai (דְּבַר יְהוָה) = word of the LORD.

items: ELI5. A Hebrew noun gets -im for many boys and -ot for many girls. There is no word for a, and the word is is left out, so the man good means the man is good.

Every Hebrew noun has a gender. Most nouns for males and many others are masculine; many feminine nouns end in -ah or -et, such as ahavah (אַהֲבָה), love, and torah (תּוֹרָה), teaching. The plural of a masculine noun is usually -im, so melekh (מֶלֶךְ), king, becomes melakhim (מְלָכִים).

Kings. Feminine nouns usually take -ot, so torah becomes torot (תּוֹרוֹת). Natural pairs use the dual ending -ayim: yad is hand and yadayim (יָדַיִם) is two hands. Mayim (מַיִם), water, and shamayim (שָׁמַיִם), heaven, only exist in this plural shape.
To say 'the', put ha- (הַ) in front, and double the first letter of the noun when the sound allows: ha-melekh (הַמֶּלֶךְ) is the king and ha-aretz (הָאָרֶץ).

The earth. To say 'a king', just say melekh (מֶלֶךְ). Hebrew has no indefinite article. The present tense of 'to be' is also usually omitted, so ha-melekh gadol (הַמֶּלֶךְ גָּדוֹל) is literally 'the king great', meaning 'the king is great'. This is called a nominal sentence.
The Shema works this way: 'the LORD our God, the LORD one' says that the LORD is one.

Words are chained by the construct state. Put the possessed noun first, then the possessor: bet ha-melekh (בֵּית הַמֶּלֶךְ) is the house of the king, and devar adonai (דְּבַר יְהוָה) is the word of the LORD. The first noun is often slightly shortened.
Add a pronoun ending instead for 'my' or 'his': beti (בֵּיתִי), my house; beto (בֵּיתוֹ), his house; bit-kha (בֵּיתְךָ), your house.

Small words attach to the front of a noun. Ve- (וְ) means and. Be- (בְּ) means in or with, le- (לְ) means to or for, and min (מִן) or mi- (מִ) means from. So be-reshit (בְּרֵאשִׁית) is in beginning, which opens Genesis.
Another handy prefix is ha- (הַ) for the article, so ba-bayit (בַּבַּיִת) is in the house. Learn these as sounds first, then spot them at the start of words as you read.
The typical sentence order is verb, subject, object, which differs from English. In the first line of Genesis, bara elohim (בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים) means created God.
Adjectives follow their nouns and agree in gender and number: ish tov (אִישׁ טוֹב), a good man; ishah tovah (אִשָּׁה טוֹבָה), a good woman; anashim tovim (אֲנָשִׁים טוֹבִים), good men.

chapters.title: Hebrew grammar: verbs, roots and pronouns

maps.title: Hebrew verbs
links: Pronoun | attaches | To nouns and verbs

summary: Hebrew verbs are built on roots of three consonants. Vowel patterns and prefixes turn the root into a tense or a stem. The two basic tenses are the perfect (completed) and the imperfect (incomplete).
Seven stems, called binyanim, give the basic, intensive, causative and reflexive meanings of the same root. Pronoun endings attach to nouns (my, your) and to prepositions.
The lab builds the perfect paradigm from a root in Python.

glossary.def: The three consonants that carry the core meaning of a word family.
A tense for completed actions, formed with suffixes; katav (כָּתַב), he wrote.
A tense for incomplete or future actions, formed with prefixes; yikhtov (יִכְתֹּב), he will write.
One of seven verb stems, such as Qal (simple), Piel (intensive), Hiphil (causative).
A vav at the start of a verb that turns it into the next step of a story.

keyPoints: Root k-t-v: katav (כָּתַב) wrote, ktav (כְּתָב) writing, mikhtav (מִכְתָּב) letter, sofer (סוֹפֵר) scribe.
Perfect suffixes: -ti I, -ta you (m), - he, -ah she, -nu we, -u they.
Imperfect prefixes: e- I, ti- you, yi- he, ni- we.
Seven binyanim: Qal, Niphal, Piel, Pual, Hiphil, Hophal, Hitpael.
Vayomer (וַיֹּאמֶר) = and he said: vav plus imperfect tells a story in sequence.
Pronouns: ani (אֲנִי) I, atah (אַתָּה) you, hu he, hi she, anachnu (אֲנַחְנוּ) we, hem they.

items: ELI5. A Hebrew verb grows from three letters like a plant from a seed. Add little bits to the front and back and it tells you who did it and when.

Hebrew vocabulary is easiest to see through roots. The three letters k-t-v give the sense of writing: katav (כָּתַב), he wrote; ktav (כְּתָב), writing; mikhtav (מִכְתָּב), a letter; sofer (סוֹפֵר), scribe (related).
The root sh-m-r means guarding: shamar (שָׁמַר), he guarded; mishmar (מִשְׁמָר), a watch. The root sh-l-m gives shalom (שָׁלוֹם), peace, shalem (שָׁלֵם).
Whole, and Shlomo (שְׁלֹמֹה), Solomon. Learning a root unlocks a whole family.

lesson.code:
katavti כָּתַבְתִּי   I wrote        katavnu כָּתַבְנוּ   we wrote
katavta כָּתַבְתָּ   you wrote (m)  ketavtem כְּתַבְתֶּם  you wrote (pl)
katavt כָּתַבְתְּ    you wrote (f)
katav כָּתַב     he wrote        katvu כָּתְבוּ     they wrote
katvah כָּתְבָה    she wrote

items: The perfect tense describes an action that is finished. You add a suffix to the stem: -ti for I, -ta for you, nothing for he, -ah for she, -nu for we, -u for they.
Notice that the vowel in the stem shortens when a vowel suffix is added, so katav (כָּתַב) becomes katvah (כָּתְבָה) and katvu (כָּתְבוּ). The imperfect tense uses prefixes: ekhtov (אֶכְתֹּב).
I will write; tikhtov (תִּכְתֹּב), you will write; yikhtov (יִכְתֹּב), he will write; nikhtov (נִכְתֹּב), we will write.

A Hebrew verb also has a stem, called a binyan. The basic one is the Qal: katav (כָּתַב), he wrote. The Niphal is often passive, nikhtav (נִכְתַּב), it was written. The Piel makes an intensive sense, so lamad (לָמַד), he learned, becomes limed (לִמֵּד), he taught.
The Hiphil is causative: malakh (מָלַךְ), he reigned, becomes himlikh (הִמְלִיךְ).
He made king. The other three, Pual, Hophal and Hitpael, are passive and reflexive counterparts.

In stories the verb often begins with vav. Vayomer elohim (וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹהִים) means and God said. A vav joined to an imperfect form turns it into a past narrative: and he said, and he saw, and he went. This is the backbone of Genesis.
The pronouns are ani (אֲנִי), I; atah (אַתָּה), you (m); at (אַתְּ), you (f); hu (הוּא), he; hi (הִיא), she; anachnu (אֲנַחְנוּ).
We; atem (אַתֶּם), you (pl); hem (הֵם), they. They attach as endings: -i my, -kha your, -o his, -ah her, -enu our. So Elohenu (אֱלֹהֵינוּ) is our God, from elohim (אֱלֹהִים) and -enu.

links: Sigma Σ σ ς | has | A final form

summary: Greek has 24 letters, each with a capital and a small form, and it reads left to right. You already know many of them from mathematics: alpha (Α α), beta (Β β), pi (Π π), sigma (Σ σ ς), omega (Ω ω).

Words that begin with a vowel carry a breathing mark: smooth (no h) or rough (an h sound). Marks above the word show stress and are learned with each word. Diphthongs like ou and ai give single sounds.
The labs match letters and compute isopsephy, the Greek counterpart of gematria.

glossary.def: A sign over an initial vowel: rough (h) or smooth (no h).
Two vowels pronounced as one sound, like ai or ou.
The form ς used for sigma (Σ σ ς) at the end of a word.
A mark (acute, grave or circumflex) showing which syllable is stressed.
Adding the number values of the Greek letters in a word.

keyPoints: 24 letters: alpha (Α α) to omega (Ω ω), left to right.
Final sigma ς appears only at the end of a word.
Rough breathing ῾ means an h before the vowel; smooth ᾿ means none.
Diphthongs: ai, ei, oi, au, eu, ou.
Gamma (Γ γ) before gamma, kappa (Κ κ), xi (Ξ ξ) or chi (Χ χ) sounds like n: aggelos is angelos.
Every word of two or more syllables carries an accent.

items: ELI5. Greek has 24 letters, and you know some from maths class: alpha, pi, omega. A little h mark on a vowel tells you to breathe out before you say it.
The Greek alphabet came from the Phoenician alphabet, the same family as Hebrew, but Greek added letters for vowels.

It has 24 letters: alpha (Α α), beta (Β β), gamma (Γ γ), delta (Δ δ), epsilon (Ε ε), zeta (Ζ ζ), eta (Η η), theta (Θ θ), iota (Ι ι), kappa (Κ κ), lambda (Λ λ), mu (Μ μ), nu (Ν ν), xi (Ξ ξ), omicron (Ο ο), pi (Π π), rho (Ρ ρ), sigma (Σ σ ς), tau (Τ τ).

Upsilon (Υ υ), phi (Φ φ), chi (Χ χ), psi (Ψ ψ) and omega (Ω ω). Each has a capital and a small form. Most capitals look like English letters, but beware Rho, which looks like P and sounds like r, and Eta, like H but sounding like ay.

lesson.code:
Α α alpha a    | Β β beta b     | Γ γ gamma g   | Δ δ delta d
Ε ε epsilon e  | Ζ ζ zeta z     | Η η eta e(ay) | Θ θ theta th
Ι ι iota i     | Κ κ kappa k    | Λ λ lambda l  | Μ μ mu m
Ν ν nu n       | Ξ ξ xi x       | Ο ο omicron o | Π π pi p
Ρ ρ rho r      | Σ σ ς sigma s  | Τ τ tau t     | Υ υ upsilon u(y)
Φ φ phi ph     | Χ χ chi kh     | Ψ ψ psi ps    | Ω ω omega o(long)

items: Some sounds need two letters in English. Theta (Θ θ) is th, phi (Φ φ) is ph or f, chi (Χ χ) is kh as in Scottish loch, and psi (Ψ ψ) is ps. The letter sigma (Σ σ ς) has two small shapes: σ in the middle of a word and ς at the end, as in λόγος.
Gamma (Γ γ) before another gamma, kappa (Κ κ), xi (Ξ ξ) or chi sounds like n, so ἄγγελος, messenger, is angelos, the source of our word angel.
A word that starts with a vowel carries a breathing mark. The rough breathing, which looks like a small backwards comma, adds an h sound: ὁ is ho (ὁ).
And ἡμέρα is hemera (ἡμέρα). The smooth breathing, like a small comma, adds nothing. A word starting with rho (Ρ ρ) always takes a rough breathing, giving the sound rh.
Some vowel pairs, the diphthongs, are one sound: αι as in 'aisle', ει as in 'eight', οι as in 'oil', αυ as in 'cow', ευ as in 'eh-oo' and ου as in 'soup'.

Accents are three little marks: acute ´, grave ` and circumflex ˜. They record where the stress falls. Beginners do not need to master the rules yet; learn each word with its accents, as you would the spelling of an English word.

Greek letters also serve as numbers: alpha (Α α) is 1, beta (Β β) 2, up to iota (Ι ι) 10, then kappa (Κ κ) 20, and so on to omega (Ω ω) 800. The isopsephy lab adds up a word's letters, like gematria in Hebrew.

chapters.title: Greek grammar: nouns, articles and cases
summary: Greek nouns have gender (masculine, feminine, neuter), number and one of five cases. The case, not the position, shows the role: nominative for the subject, accusative for the object, genitive for 'of', dative for 'to or for' and vocative for calling out.
The article (the) changes with the noun, and it agrees in gender, number and case. Prepositions take certain cases, and the case changes the meaning.
The labs match case to function and build the endings of a typical noun.

glossary.def: The form of a noun that shows its job in the sentence.
The case of the subject.
The case showing possession or 'of'.
The case of the indirect object: to, for, in, by.
The case of the direct object.
The case used to address someone.

keyPoints: Five cases: nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, vocative.
Article (nominative): ho (ὁ) masculine, he feminine, to neuter; ton (τόν), ten, to in the accusative.
Second declension masculine: logos (λόγος), logou (λόγου), logo (λόγῳ), logon (λόγον).
First declension feminine: agape (ἀγάπη), agapes (ἀγάπης), agape, agapen (ἀγάπην).
Plural nominative: logoi (λόγοι), agapai (ἀγάπαι).
Word order is flexible because endings show roles.

items: ELI5. In Greek the ending on a word tells you its job, like a name tag. Because of the tags, you can shuffle the words and the meaning stays the same.
In English, 'the dog bites the man' and 'the man bites the dog' differ only by word order. In Greek, the endings show who bites whom. The subject takes the nominative, the object the accusative.
In the sentence ho theos agapa ton kosmon (ὁ θεὸς ἀγαπᾷ τὸν κόσμον), God loves the world, ho theos (ὁ θεός), God, is nominative and ton kosmon (τὸν κόσμον).
The world, is accusative. You could shuffle the words and the meaning would not change.

lesson.code:
masc    fem    neut
nominative   ho ὁ      he ἡ     to τό
genitive     tou τοῦ     tes τῆς    tou τοῦ
dative       to τό      te τῇ     to τό
accusative   ton τόν     ten τήν    to τό

items: The article changes in the same way, and it tells you the gender, number and case at a glance. A typical masculine noun of the second declension is logos (λόγος), word.

Its singular is logos (nominative), logou (λόγου) (genitive, of the word), logo (λόγῳ) (dative, to the word) and logon (λόγον) (accusative), and its vocative is loge (λόγε). The plural is logoi (λόγοι).
Logon, logois (λόγοις) and logous (λόγους). A typical feminine noun of the first declension is agape (ἀγάπη), love: agape, agapes (ἀγάπης), agape, agapen (ἀγάπην). The plural begins agapai (ἀγάπαι).

lesson.code:
logos λόγος   word (sg)     logoi λόγοι    words (pl)
logou λόγου   of the word    logon λόγον    of the words
logo λόγῳ    to the word    logois λόγοις   to the words
logon λόγον   the word (obj) logous λόγους   the words (obj)

items: The cases cover a wide range of meanings. The genitive is of, so tou theou (τοῦ θεοῦ) is of God. The dative is to, for, in or by, so to logo (τῷ λόγῳ) is by the word. The accusative is the object, and also direction, so pros ton theon (πρὸς τὸν θεόν) is toward God.
Prepositions take certain cases, and the case alters the sense: dia (διά) with the genitive is through, but with the accusative it is because of. Learn each preposition with its case.

chapters.title: Greek grammar: verbs

maps.title: Greek verbs
links: Participle | acts | As verb and adjective

summary: A Greek verb shows tense, voice, mood, person and number. Tense in Greek is as much about the kind of action (ongoing, simple, completed) as about time.
The regular present active has endings -ō, -eis, -ei, -omen, -ete, -ousi. Past tenses add an augment (e-) at the front. Voice can be active, middle or passive. The verb 'to be' is irregular.
The lab conjugates the present of regular verbs.

glossary.def: When or how an action takes place: present, imperfect, future, aorist, perfect.
A past tense for a simple, single event.
Whether the subject acts (active), acts on itself (middle), or is acted on (passive).
The way a statement is made: indicative, subjunctive, optative, imperative.
An e- added to the front of a past-tense indicative verb.
A verb form that works like an adjective, such as 'loving'.

keyPoints: Present active of luo (λύω): luo, lueis (λύεις), luei (λύει), luomen (λύομεν), luete (λύετε), luousi (λύουσι).
Imperfect: eluon (ἔλυον), ongoing past; aorist: eluse (ἔλυσε), simple past.
Future: luso (λύσω); perfect: leluka, a past act with present result.
Voices: active, middle, passive. Moods: indicative, subjunctive, optative, imperative.
Eimi (εἰμί), to be: eimi, ei, esti (ἐστί), esmen (ἐσμέν), este (ἐστέ), eisi (εἰσί).
The verb form shows the person, so the subject pronoun is often left out.

items: ELI5. Greek verbs wear endings for I, you and they. A little e at the front means it happened before. Some verbs even act on themselves, which English cannot do.
Greek verbs are rich, but their core is regular. We learn them on a model verb, luo (λύω).

Which means loose or release. Remove the ending -o to find the stem lu-. The present active indicative adds -o for I, -eis for you, -ei for he or she, -omen for we, -ete for you all and -ousi for they.
So luo is I loose, lueis (λύεις) you loose, luei (λύει) he looses, luomen (λύομεν) we loose, luete (λύετε) you loose and luousi (λύουσι) they loose.

lesson.code:
luo λύω    I loose        luomen λύομεν  we loose
lueis λύεις  you loose      luete λύετε   you (pl) loose
luei λύει   he looses      luousi λύουσι  they loose

items: Because the ending shows the person, the pronoun is usually left out: agapo se (ἀγαπῶ σε) means I love you, with the pronoun se (σέ, you) as the object. Tense in Greek is about the kind of action.

The present means ongoing or repeated, the aorist is a simple event, and the perfect is a finished action with lasting results. In the indicative, past tenses add an augment, a small e- in front of the stem: eluon (ἔλυον) (imperfect, I was loosing) and eluse (ἔλυσε) (aorist, he loosed).
The future adds -s-: luso (λύσω), I will loose.
Voice shows the relationship between the subject and the action. In the active voice the subject acts: luo (λύω), I loose. In the passive the subject receives it: luomai (λύομαι).
I am being loosed. In the middle voice, found in Greek and not in English, the subject acts on or for itself: luomai can also mean I loose for myself.
The moods include the indicative for facts, the subjunctive for possibilities, the optative for wishes and the imperative for commands, as in luson (λῦσον), loose!
The verb to be, eimi (εἰμί), is irregular and very frequent: eimi, I am; ei (εἶ), you are; esti(n) (ἐστί(ν)), he or she is; esmen (ἐσμέν), we are; este (ἐστέ), you are; eisi(n) (εἰσί(ν)), they are.
We have seen it in John 1:1 as en (ἦν), was, and in 1 John 4:8, ho theos agape estin (ὁ θεὸς ἀγάπη ἐστίν). Participles, such as agapon (ἀγαπῶν).
Loving, act as both verbs and adjectives and are the most common way of building longer sentences in the New Testament.

chapters.title: Latin: sounds, nouns and cases
summary: Latin uses the same letters as English, so you can start reading at once. The Church pronounces them softly (ci as chi) and the classical way is harder (ci as ki); this course uses the Church reading. Latin has no word for 'the' or 'a'.

Nouns have gender and number and six cases: nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, ablative and vocative. Five declensions group the nouns by their endings. Adjectives agree with their noun in gender, number and case. The verb tends to come last.
The labs decline the first declension and match cases to their functions.

glossary.def: A group of nouns that share the same set of case endings.
A case for by, with, from or in; the 'by means of' case.
The pronunciation used in the Church, close to Italian.
Adjectives match their noun's gender, number and case.
The part of the word that stays the same when endings change.

keyPoints: Church sounds: c before e or i is 'ch'; ae and oe are 'e'; gn is 'ny'; j and i are 'y'.
No articles: puella means girl, a girl or the girl.
Six cases: nom, gen, dat, acc, abl, voc.
First declension (puella): -a -ae -ae -am -a; plural -ae -arum -is -as -is.
Second declension (dominus): -us -i -o -um -o; voc -e.
Stress: the next-to-last syllable if it is long or closed, otherwise the one before it.

items: ELI5. Latin looks friendly because it uses our letters. Nouns have six name tags called cases, and there is no word for the or a, so you have to look at the endings.

Latin looks easy, because its alphabet is yours. There are 23 letters, without j, u and w, which came later. Pronunciation has two traditions. Classical Latin, as Caesar spoke it, says c as k, v as w, and ae as in 'eye'.

Church Latin, used in the Vulgate readings and hymns, says ci as chi, ce as che, v as v and ae as e. Church Latin sounds close to Italian. We use it here: Caelum is chay-lum, Deus is day-oos, and Pax Vobiscum is pahks vo-bees-kum.

Stress is predictable. In a word of two syllables, stress the first: Do-mi-nus has three, so look at the next-to-last. If that syllable is long (a long vowel, or a vowel followed by two consonants), stress it. Otherwise stress the one before it.
So do-MI-nus, since the i is long, but A-ni-ma, with a short i.

Nouns have six cases, as in Greek (plus the ablative). The nominative is the subject, the genitive means 'of', the dative 'to or for', the accusative is the object, the ablative 'by, with, from, in' and the vocative is for calling. The first declension has endings -a, -ae, -ae, -am, -a.
So puella, girl, goes: puella (nom), puellae (of the girl), puellae (to the girl).
Puellam (the girl as object), puella (by the girl). The plural is puellae, puellarum, puellis, puellas, puellis.

Adjectives take the same endings and match their noun: Deus bonus, a good God; filia bona, a good daughter; verbum bonum, a good word. Prepositions take the accusative (ad, to; in, into; per, through) or the ablative (in, in; cum, with; de, about; ex, from).
Latin has no articles, and the word order is flexible: Deus creavit caelum and caelum creavit Deus both mean that God created heaven.

chapters.title: Latin grammar: verbs
summary: Latin verbs belong to four conjugations, told apart by the vowel before -re in the infinitive: amare, monere, regere, audire. Personal endings -o, -s, -t, -mus, -tis, -nt show the person, so the pronoun is not needed.
Each verb is listed with four principal parts from which every form can be built. The tenses include the present, imperfect, future and perfect. The verb sum, to be, is irregular and common.
The lab conjugates a first-conjugation verb in Python.

glossary.def: A group of verbs sharing the same pattern of endings.
Four forms listed in the dictionary, from which all others are built.
The 'to' form: amare, to love.
A past tense for ongoing action: amabat, he was loving.
A past tense for a completed act: amavit, he loved.

keyPoints: Present of amo: amo, amas, amat, amamus, amatis, amant.
Four conjugations: amare, monere, regere, audire.
Sum: sum, es, est, sumus, estis, sunt; imperfect eram, erat; perfect fui.
Perfect endings: -i, -isti, -it, -imus, -istis, -erunt.
Principal parts of amo: amo, amare, amavi, amatum.
Imperative: ama! (love!), audi! (hear!).

items: ELI5. A Latin verb carries its own who. Amamus is we love, all in one word. The verb likes to sit at the end of the sentence, like a period at the end.

A Latin verb contains a lot in one word. Amamus means we love. The ending -mus says we, so no pronoun is needed. The four conjugations differ by the vowel in the infinitive. The first is -are, as in amare, to love. The second is -ere with a long e, as in monere, to warn.
The third is -ere with a short e, as in regere, to rule. The fourth is -ire, as in audire, to hear. Each takes the same personal endings.

lesson.code:
amo      I love         amamus   we love
amas     you love       amatis   you (pl) love
amat     he/she loves   amant    they love

items: The personal endings are -o or -m for I, -s for you, -t for he or she, -mus for we, -tis for you all and -nt for they. The vowel before them depends on the conjugation: amas, mones, regis, audis. The verb is listed in a dictionary by four principal parts: amo (I love), amare (to love).
Amavi (I loved) and amatum (loved). From these you can build every form. The perfect uses its own endings: amavi, amavisti, amavit, amavimus, amavistis, amaverunt.

The verb sum, to be, is irregular: sum, es, est, sumus, estis, sunt. The imperfect is eram, eras, erat and the perfect fui, fuisti, fuit. It appears in John 1:1 as erat: in principio erat Verbum, in the beginning was the Word.
Latin puts the verb at the end of the clause more often than not: Deus caelum creavit, God heaven created. The Vulgate often follows the Greek order, though, so the verb sometimes comes earlier.

The imperative gives commands. The singular is the stem: ama, love! audi, hear! as in the Shema, Audi, Israel. Add -te for the plural: amate, audite. The passive voice has its own endings, such as amatur, he is loved. The passive explains forms in the Bible like facta est, was made.
Participles and the subjunctive come later, but even now you can read simple verse once you know the person endings and sum.

chapters.title: Comparing the three: pronouns, numbers and 'to be'
summary: The same ideas are expressed in different ways in the three languages. This chapter lays them side by side: pronouns, numbers 1 to 10, the verb 'to be', questions and negatives.
Hebrew has one article and no case endings, Greek has an article and five cases, and Latin has no article and six cases. Seeing the contrasts makes each language easier to remember.
The labs ask you to match the same word across the three languages.

glossary.def: A word like I or you that stands for a noun.
A word that denies: lo, ou, non.
A number word.
Hebrew ha- (הַ), Greek ho (ὁ)/he/to; Latin has none.
The linking verb 'to be'.

keyPoints: I: ani (אֲנִי), ego (ἐγώ), ego; you: atah (אַתָּה), su, tu; we: anachnu (אֲנַחְנוּ), hemeis (ἡμεῖς), nos.
To be: Hebrew leaves it out in the present, Greek eimi (εἰμί), Latin sum.
No/not: lo, ou(k) or me, non.
Question words: who mi, tis, quis; what mah, ti, quid; where eifo (אֵיפֹה), pou, ubi.
Numbers 1 to 10 side by side are below.
An article tells definiteness; Latin relies on context.

items: ELI5. Put the three side by side: I is ego in Greek and Latin, and ani in Hebrew. Hebrew skips is, Greek says eimi, Latin says sum. Numbers like six look the same in Greek and Latin.

Seeing the three side by side shows both the differences and the surprising family ties. The English 'I' is ego (ἐγώ) in both Greek and Latin, as in 'ego' in English. Hebrew uses ani (אֲנִי). 'You' is atah (אַתָּה, masculine singular) in Hebrew, su (σύ) in Greek and tu in Latin.
Notice that Greek su (σύ) and Latin tu are close cousins, while Hebrew uses a different root. 'We' is anachnu (אֲנַחְנוּ), hemeis (ἡμεῖς) and nos.

En (ἦν, Greek, from eimi) and erat (Latin) all mean was. Note the match in John 1:1: Greek en ho logos (ἦν ὁ λόγος) and Latin erat Verbum. The articles also differ. Hebrew attaches ha- (הַ) to a noun. Greek has ho (ὁ), he, to.

chapters.title: Core vocabulary I: nouns in three languages
summary: Thirty common nouns, each in Hebrew, Greek and Latin, with a memory hook. Many of them became English words through Greek and Latin, which makes them easy to remember.

The flashcard lab uses Leitner boxes: you move up a box when you know a card and back to box 1 when you miss it. You can choose any direction, such as English to Hebrew or Greek to Latin, so that you can translate between the languages directly.
Three matching labs drill the words in groups.

glossary.def: A link between a new word and something you already know.
A level in a spaced-repetition system; the higher the box, the longer you wait.
A word copied from another language, like amen or hallelujah.
An English word built from a Greek or Latin one, like theology.
Retrieving a word from memory without looking.

keyPoints: Learn 5 words at a time and revisit them tomorrow.
Say each word aloud with its English hook.
Greek and Latin give English hundreds of words; Hebrew gives shalom (שָׁלוֹם), amen, sabbath.
Reverse the direction once you know a card.
Review every day, a little, instead of once a week for a long time.

items: ELI5. Thirty nouns, each with a picture trick: photo for light, pacify for peace, Bethlehem for bread. Flip flashcards every day and they stick.

The nouns in this list are the core of the Bible's vocabulary: God, Lord, man, woman, father, mother, son, day, night, light, water, earth, heaven, word, love, life, death, king, house, peace, spirit, name, people, hand, heart, truth, bread, city, sin and book.
For each one you get the Hebrew, the Greek and the Latin with a short hook. Learn them in groups of five, and say the three forms together, aloud.

Here are some memory stories. Light: Greek phos gives us photo, a picture made from light, and Latin lux gives lucid. Peace: Latin pax gives pacify and Pacific, the peaceful ocean, and the Hebrew shalom (שָׁלוֹם) has a close Arabic cousin, salaam.

Bread: Latin panis gives pantry, and the Hebrew lechem (לֶחֶם) hides in Bethlehem, house of bread. Heart: Greek kardia (καρδία) is cardiac and Latin cor is cordial and core. Word: Greek logos (λόγος) gives logic and dialogue, Latin verbum gives verb and verbal.

The first group is God, Lord, man, woman, father. The Greek theos (θεός) gives theology and the Latin Deus gives deity. The Greek anthropos (ἄνθρωπος) gives anthropology; the Latin homo gives human. The Greek pater (πατήρ) and Latin pater are twins; both give paternal.
The Hebrew av is the same as the Aramaic abba. The second group is mother, son, day, night, light. Greek meter (μήτηρ) and Latin mater share a root with English mother.
Notice that Greek and Latin words often resemble English words in the same family, but Hebrew words need the repetition and the story.

Use the flashcards every day. The deck is chosen at the top, as are the two languages: pick English and Hebrew, then flip it to Hebrew and English. Missing a card sends it back to box 1, where you see it soon. A card you know moves up and returns later. The goal is to get twelve cards to box 3.
Short sessions of five to ten minutes are better than one long one.

summary: Fifteen of the most frequent verbs and adjectives in the Bible, in all three languages: say, see, hear, go, come, give, know, be, do, write, love, live, good, great and one.

Verbs change form: in Hebrew by root and pattern, in Greek and Latin by ending. We list the dictionary form of each (Hebrew past he-form, Greek 'I' form, Latin 'I' form) and drill them with flashcards.
The lab matches verbs across the languages and uses the cards.

glossary.def: The form under which a word is listed: Hebrew 3rd person perfect, Greek and Latin 'I' form.
The part of a verb that stays the same.
A verb whose forms do not follow the regular pattern, like sum.
A list of words ranked by how often they appear.
Words you can produce, not just recognise.

keyPoints: Hebrew lists a verb by its 3rd masculine singular perfect: amar, he said.
Greek and Latin list the 'I' form: lego, dico; Latin also gives the infinitive.
Frequent verbs are often irregular: sum, eo, do, facio.
Good and great are adjectives and agree with their nouns.
Learn a verb with a sample phrase: audi, Israel; ho theos agape estin (ὁ θεὸς ἀγάπη ἐστίν).

items: ELI5. Verbs are the doing words: say, see, hear, go, give, love. Learn each with a mini phrase like Audi, Israel, and you will remember them in context.

A small number of verbs make up a large part of the Bible. To say, see, hear, go, come, give, know and be cover most of the stories, and to love is the big word of the New Testament. Learn these, and you can follow a lot of the text.
The Hebrew dictionary form is the third masculine singular perfect: amar, he said; raah, he saw; shama (שָׁמַע).
He heard. The Greek and Latin dictionary form is the first person: lego, dico; horao (ὁράω), video; akouo (ἀκούω), audio.
Some of these have clear hooks. Latin video gives video and vision; audio gives audio and audience; dico gives dictate and diction; scribo gives scribe and script; vivo gives vivid.

Greek grapho (γράφω) gives graph and graphic; ginosko (γινώσκω) gives agnostic, one who does not know; poieo (ποιέω) gives poem and poet, a maker. The Hebrew verbs ask for the story technique: halakh (הָלַךְ), he went, lives on in the word Halakha, the way one walks.
Natan (נָתַן), he gave, is in names like Nathan and Jonathan.
Adjectives follow their nouns in Hebrew and agree with them: tov (טוֹב), good; gadol (גָּדוֹל).

Great. In Greek agathos (ἀγαθός) and megas (μέγας) follow the article and noun pattern, so ho (ὁ) agathos anthropos (ἄνθρωπος) is the good man. In Latin bonus, magnus and unus change with the noun. Good is a nice test: Deus bonus, filia bona, verbum bonum.
The Hebrew phrase mazal tov, good luck, uses tov, good, and Latin bene is good in 'benefit' and 'benediction'.

Learn a verb together with a little phrase. Audi, Israel gives audio. Ho (ὁ) theos (θεός) agape (ἀγάπη) estin (ἐστίν) gives you eimi (εἰμί), estin. Dixit Deus: Fiat lux gives dico and facio. Vayomer elohim (וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹהִים) gives amar. The flashcards in this chapter use the Verbs deck.
Run it in both directions, and then try going from Greek to Latin, which trains you to translate directly.

chapters.title: Conversational phrases

maps.title: Everyday phrases
links: Thank you | is | toda, eucharisto, gratias

summary: Sixteen useful phrases: greetings, thanks, yes and no, asking a name, asking where, and a few blessings. Each is given in Hebrew, Greek and Latin so you can say it in whichever language you like.
Most of these phrases are formed from the vocabulary and grammar you have seen. Hebrew and Greek greetings were wishes of peace and joy. Latin greetings wish health.
The flashcard lab includes a Phrases deck. Go through it in both directions.

glossary.def: A word or phrase to meet someone.
A word or phrase to part.
A wish of good for someone.
The form used to give a command or wish: salve, vale.
The level of formality of language.

keyPoints: Shalom (שָׁלוֹם), chaire (χαῖρε), salve open a conversation.
Shalom (שָׁלוֹם) aleichem, eirene (εἰρήνη) hymin, pax vobis: peace be with you.
Toda (תּוֹדָה), eucharisto (εὐχαριστῶ), gratias: thank you.
Mah shimkha, ti onoma (ὄνομα) soi, quod nomen tibi est: what is your name?
Te amo, agapo se (ἀγαπῶ σε), ani (אֲנִי) ohev otkha: I love you.
Barukh elohim (אֱלֹהִים), eulogetos ho (ὁ) theos (θεός), benedictus Deus: blessed be God.

items: ELI5. Hello is shalom, chaire or salve, and each one is a little wish: peace, joy or health. Say them out loud to a friend, because words you use stay.

A language is easiest to learn if you use it. Begin with greetings. In Hebrew you say shalom (שָׁלוֹם), peace; in Greek chaire (χαῖρε), rejoice, which is also the word an angel says to Mary; in Latin salve, be well.
For parting, Hebrew says lekh leshalom, go in peace, Greek says errhoso, be strong, and Latin says vale, be strong and well. The idea is the same in each: a wish for the other's wellbeing.

The blessing peace be with you is shalom (שָׁלוֹם) aleichem in Hebrew, eirene (εἰρήνη) hymin in Greek and pax vobis in Latin. In the Mass, pax vobiscum, peace be with you, is the same wish. Thanks is toda (תּוֹדָה) in Hebrew, eucharisto (εὐχαριστῶ) in Greek, and gratias in Latin.
The Greek word became the Eucharist, the thanksgiving, and the Latin gives gratitude. Please is bevakasha (בְּבַקָּשָׁה), parakalo (παρακαλῶ) and quaeso.

To ask a name, Hebrew says mah shimkha, what your name. Greek says ti onoma (ὄνομα) soi, what name to you. Latin says quod nomen tibi est, what name to you is. To answer, use the same pattern: shemi, my name; onoma moi, name to me; nomen mihi est, name to me is.

Notice how the Greek and Latin both use the dative, to me, while the Hebrew attaches the ending -i. The question words from the previous chapter, mi, tis, quis, mah, ti, quid, eifo (אֵיפֹה), pou and ubi, now appear in sentences.
Finally, a few phrases of faith. Barukh elohim (אֱלֹהִים), eulogetos ho (ὁ) theos (θεός).

Benedictus Deus is blessed be God. Deus caritas est, God is love, from 1 John 4:8, is ho theos agape estin (ὁ θεὸς ἀγάπη ἐστίν) in Greek. The Hebrew line, a plain rendering, is not a verse of the Hebrew Bible.
Say the phrases out loud, and try answering a greeting in a different language than the one you heard. That is the quickest way to become comfortable with all three.

chapters.title: Reading with an interlinear

maps.title: Interlinear reading
links: Parallel texts | show | The same idea

summary: An interlinear shows the original word, its sound, and a gloss, one under the other. It lets you read real verses before you know the whole grammar.

The reader lab holds thirteen passages: Genesis 1:1 in Hebrew, Greek and Latin, John 1:1 in Greek and Latin, Genesis 1:3, the Shema, Psalm 23:1, 1 John 4:8 and the Pater (πατήρ) Noster. Tap a word to see its sound and meaning, then show the smooth translation and the grammar notes.
You learn the most by comparing: the same verse in three languages.

glossary.def: A text with each word glossed directly beneath.
A short English meaning attached to a word.
Two or more versions of the same text side by side.
A natural English version of the whole sentence.
Naming the part of speech, case, tense, person and so on of a word.

keyPoints: Read the original aloud before you look at the gloss.
Tap each word: sound, then meaning.
Find the verb first, then the subject, then the object.
Compare the same verse in two languages.
Parse the endings you know: case for nouns, person for verbs.

items: ELI5. An interlinear puts a tiny English word under each foreign word, like training wheels. You can read a real verse before you know all the grammar.

A good way to begin reading is an interlinear. Each word of the original is shown with its sound and a short English gloss. You see Hebrew bereshit (בְּרֵאשִׁית) bara elohim (בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים) as in-beginning, created, God.
The reading order stays that of the original, which teaches you to think in Hebrew, Greek or Latin order rather than English order.

Take Genesis 1:1 in three languages. In Hebrew, bereshit (בְּרֵאשִׁית) bara elohim (בָּרָא אֱלֹהִים) et hashamayim ve-et ha-arets: in-beginning created God the heavens and the earth. The verb comes first.

In Greek, en arche epoiesen ho (ὁ) theos (θεός) ton (τόν) ouranon kai ten gen: in beginning made the God the heaven and the earth; the cases show ho theos as subject and ton ouranon as object. In Latin, in principio creavit Deus caelum et terram: in beginning created God heaven and earth.
In all three, the words for beginning, God, heaven and earth match the vocabulary you learned.
John 1:1 shows the connection between Greek and Latin: en arche en ho (ὁ) logos (λόγος).

Kai ho logos en pros ton theon (πρὸς τὸν θεόν); in principio erat Verbum, et Verbum erat apud Deum. The two versions follow each other word for word, since the Latin translators kept the Greek order. The Shema has the Hebrew nominal sentence, with no verb: the LORD our God, the LORD one.
The Latin adds est. The Greek adds the verb estin (ἐστίν) in the Septuagint as well.

Here is a routine. First read the original aloud. Second, tap each word and say its gloss. Third, spot the verb and the subject. Fourth, look at the notes for a grammar point. Fifth, show the smooth translation and compare it with your own guess.
Open all thirteen passages to finish the lab, then come back and read them again without the glosses. That is when you will notice how much you now recognise.

chapters.title: Translating and remembering
summary: A reliable method for translating a sentence: find the verb, find the subject, use the endings to work out the roles, gloss each word literally, then smooth into good English. The same steps work for Hebrew, Greek and Latin.

Translating between the languages teaches you quickly, because you compare structures: the same idea turns up with different grammar. Cognates and hooks help you remember, and spaced repetition makes it last.
The labs include a Leitner scheduler in Python and a translation exercise.

glossary.def: A word-for-word translation that keeps the original order.
A natural version in good English.
Reviewing at increasing intervals to build long memory.
A memory aid, like a rhyme, picture or hook.
The method of placing items in a familiar place in your mind.

keyPoints: Method: verb, subject, object, endings, literal gloss, smooth English.
Compare the same sentence in three languages to see the structure.
Use hooks: connect to English words, pictures and stories.
Space your reviews: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 days.
Say words aloud, and write them by hand.
Use the words in your own sentences.

items: ELI5. To translate, find the doing word first, then who did it, then what they did it to. Then say it in good English. For remembering, review a word after one day, two, four and eight.

To translate, follow a method. Step one: find the verb. In Hebrew, it is often first. In Latin, it is often last. In Greek, it can be anywhere. Step two: find the subject. In Greek and Latin it is in the nominative; in Hebrew it usually follows the verb.

Step three: find the objects, using endings or the Hebrew object marker et. Step four: gloss each remaining word literally. Step five: write a smooth English version. Never skip the literal gloss, because it shows you what the original really says.

Try a Latin example. Deus creavit caelum et terram. Verb: creavit, he created. Subject: Deus, in the nominative. Objects: caelum and terram, both in the accusative, joined by et, and. Smooth: God created heaven and earth. Now try the Greek: ho (ὁ) theos (θεός) ten gen epoiesen.
The article ho is nominative, so theos is the subject; ten gen is accusative feminine, the object; epoiesen is the verb, he made. You can read it, even though the order is different from the Latin.

Memory is a skill. Spaced repetition says to review a word just before you forget it: after a day, then two days, then four, eight and sixteen. The Leitner boxes you used in the flashcard lab are a physical version of this: each box has a longer wait, and a miss sends the card back to box 1.
The loci method places each word in a familiar room: put a lux, a lamp, on the table, a panis, a loaf, on the shelf. Hooks tie a word to something you already know, such as photo for phos.
Make the languages work together. A Latin word often tells you a Greek one: sex and hex, septem and hepta (ἑπτά). Greek words show up in English theology: theos (θεός), logos (λόγος).

Kardia (καρδία). Hebrew words survive in English as amen, sabbath, hallelujah, messiah, jubilee and cherub. Write ten short sentences of your own, such as Deus est bonus, ho (ὁ) theos agathos (ἀγαθός) estin (ἐστίν). Say them out loud, and then translate each into a different language.
That is real translation practice, and it is how learners become readers.
